architect.rationale: Single-loop, four sequential slices on one branch. One app (orchestra), almost all in one crate (orchestra-core), and the slices are not 3+ disjoint: s2 and s3 both own core/src/link/mod.rs, and s3 consumes s1's subscribe/dispatch API and s2's noise/frame/store API, so it is a sequence, not a diamond. s1 and s2 have no artifact edge and are file-disjoint, but two parallel slices do not earn a fan-out. Verified on disk at e84d179: Emit/Notify are single Box closures fixed in with_writer (session/mod.rs:384-405); the only two (self.emit) sites are publish_saving (mod.rs:550-554) and publish_task (610-614), both taking emit_order while inner is held (lock order inner then emit_order), which makes an atomic snapshot+subscribe possible: take inner, read projects/sessions/inbox/tasks, take emit_order, read the seq counter, register, release. No seq exists; revision is private and skips text-only lines. dispatch_answer and the StartArgs->SessionSettings mapping are shell-only (desktop/src-tauri/src/commands.rs:46,72-80,102); storage_status returns the shell's managed StorageStatus (commands.rs:91-95). The CI guard (test.yml:34) is cargo tree -e normal,build for gtk|webkit|tauri|wry; dev-deps are never checked. core/tests/*.rs run automatically under cargo test -p orchestra-core on ubuntu-24.04 and ubuntu-24.04-arm and under cargo test --workspace on windows-latest; macOS compiles them only (cargo check --tests). test.yml needs no change. Two scout gaps found while verifying, raised as G10 and G11: the plaintext {proto,v} frame carries no pairing-vs-reconnect mode, and Noise KK needs the responder to know the initiator's static key before reading message 1, which a host with N paired clients does not. decisions_for_gate.title: Blocking vs async
decisions_for_gate.recommend: Blocking tungstenite on std threads, matching the core (no async anywhere in it). One accept thread per bound address (non-blocking listener polled ~100 ms against a stop flag); one thread per connection owning the WebSocket, reading with a short timeout (~25 ms) and draining its outgoing queue between reads; one short-lived worker per in-flight call (cap 8 per connection, then result error failed 'busy'), results back through the outgoing queue. Caps: 16 connections; 30 s write timeout then drop. On Windows a timed-out read is TimedOut (os error 10060), not WouldBlock; both mean no data and must be handled alike; the windows-latest workspace job proves it. CI guard: tungstenite with default-features=false, features=[handshake] pulls bytes, log, rand 0.10, thiserror 2, data-encoding, http, httparse, sha1; none matches gtk|webkit|tauri|wry, and no tokio.
alternatives: tokio + tokio-tungstenite in core: passes the GUI guard, but brings a runtime into a thread-based core and into orchestrad, a second concurrency model beside emit_order; rejected.
Hand-rolled mio poll loop: fewer threads, much more code; reopen only if thread count becomes a problem.

decisions_for_gate.title: Bind policy and the start/stop surface
decisions_for_gate.recommend: LinkConfig { binds: Vec<SocketAddr>, host_name, link_dir, storage: StorageStatus, limits }. Empty binds = off: start() opens nothing. Every address explicit; unspecified addresses (0.0.0.0, ::) refused by a pure validator before any socket call (BindError::Unspecified), no override in v1. start() returns the actually bound addresses (port 0 resolves for tests); stop() closes listeners and every connection and joins the threads. Also open_pairing() -> PairingOffer, confirm_pairing, reject_pairing, list_clients, set_scopes, revoke. Windows Firewall: listening on 127.0.0.1 or ::1 never prompts; the first listen on a LAN or Tailscale address by an exe with no inbound rule shows Windows Security Alert in an interactive session, and Cancel creates a block rule. P3a binds only loopback in tests, so no prompt locally or on windows-latest; P3b must warn before enabling a non-loopback address.
alternatives: Allow 0.0.0.0 when literally named (README's never-by-default permits it): reopen if a user needs it.
Interface names instead of addresses: per-OS interface enumeration; rejected for v1.

decisions_for_gate.title: Confirm-on-host seam
decisions_for_gate.recommend: Yes, the seam lands now; its UI in P3b. After IKpsk2 completes and the client's hello decrypts (proving the psk and consuming the single-use window), the core holds the connection pending and calls on_pairing_request(PendingPairing{id, client_name, fingerprint}); the host answers confirm_pairing(id, scopes) or reject_pairing(id). Reject, window expiry or stop() closes the socket with no message (indistinguishable from an unknown key). Only on confirm is the client stored and sent welcome + snapshot. decisions_for_gate.title: Framing, pairing secret and offer encoding (P2 left framing to P3)
decisions_for_gate.recommend: Plaintext {proto,v} frames are WebSocket text messages; each Noise handshake message is one WebSocket binary message. After the handshake one application message = one WebSocket binary message = a sequence of [u16 big-endian length][Noise ciphertext], each ciphertext at most 65535 bytes (plaintext chunk at most 65519). Reassembled plaintext over MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES closes the connection; tungstenite max_message_size is set to the matching ciphertext bound so memory is capped before decryption. Pairing secret: 32 random bytes used directly as the IKpsk2 psk (README's 128-bit becomes 256-bit, a strengthening, no KDF to mirror in JS). PairingOffer JSON {v:1, host_id, host_name, addrs:[ip:port], host_key hex, secret hex, expires_at ms}; host_id = hex of the first 16 bytes of SHA-256(host public key). Read-idle timeout 120 s (clients ping within 60 s).
alternatives: A more/last flag byte per Noise frame instead of WebSocket message boundaries: only needed on a non-message transport.
Keep a 128-bit secret and derive the psk with SHA-256(domain || secret): smaller QR, a KDF on both sides.

s1.$comment: RE-REVIEWS NEST, and this is the rule every reader follows. The TOP LEVEL of reviews.<slice> IS attempt 1. A re-review writes attempt_2, then attempt_3, and so on, each with the same fields as the top level. Every attempt SURVIVES PERMANENTLY - history is never overwritten, flattened, or migrated up. The LATEST attempt supplies the verdict: that is what close-run.py, brief.py and verify-state.py resolve through, and what fleetview's finalVerdict() has always shown. `ever_rejected` - did ANY attempt REJECT - is DISPLAY ONLY, forever, so a rejection stays visible after it is fixed; it must never gate anything, or the fleet stops being able to loop. NO NODE MAY REWRITE AN EARLIER ATTEMPT: a second reviewer writes its own attempt_N and leaves the ones before it alone, top-level verdict included - relocating that verdict would destroy the history the board keeps and leave a key stamped written_by:reviewer with someone else as its real author. The KEY INDEX numbers an attempt, not the `attempt` field inside it; the field is display. An EMPTY attempt_N is not a re-review, it is a key nobody wrote - write the whole attempt or none of it. The walk STOPS AT THE FIRST GAP, so an attempt_3 with no attempt_2 is ignored and the earlier verdict stands: A GAP IS MALFORMED AND NO NODE MAY LEAVE ONE. Write the next UNUSED N and never skip - a mis-numbered re-review is not reported anywhere, it is simply unread, and a REJECT nobody reads is a REJECT nobody acts on. The cap is attempt_9, matching fleetview's `for (i = 2; i < 10; i++)` exactly so the two readers cannot disagree; attempt_10 and beyond is reported loudly and resolved by nobody.

findings.issue: host_key's contents are not written atomically. create_new is followed by write_all and sync_all on the real path, with no temp file and rename. A crash, kill or ENOSPC between the open and the sync leaves a 0 to 31 byte host_key, and from then on every load_or_create returns BadFile until someone deletes the file by hand. Likewise, a second process that loses the create_new race can read the half-written file and get BadFile. This fails closed: the mode is 0600 from open(2) on, so the key is never exposed and never silently replaced. A temp file created 0600 with create_new and then hard-linked or renamed into place would close the gap. Not a blocker: G4 asks for create_new with 0600, and in P3a one host loads the key once.

KK trial decryption builds a fresh HandshakeState for every candidate and drops it after a failed read, so no state carries over from one trial to the next. It returns early on a match, though, so a NoMatch takes time proportional to the number of paired clients. That leaks the count (at most 32), not any key, and only a holder of the matching private key can trigger the match path. The per-IP handshake rate limit bounds the DH cost. Acceptable; noted.

The host-side half of ikpsk2_wrong_psk_never_reaches_a_transport_message decrypts 40 zero bytes, which would fail under any key, so it proves nothing about the psk. The real property holds and is tested: in IKpsk2 the psk is mixed at the end of message 2, so an initiator with the wrong psk fails to read message 2 (asserted) and can never produce a valid first transport message. core/tests/link.rs:95 wrong_psk_closes_silently covers the end-to-end case. The documented deviation is inherent to the pattern.

Zeroization is best-effort, and the docs claim more. random_bytes leaves the array it returns on the stack, Psk::from_bytes(*expose()) in pairing.rs:50 makes unwiped temporaries, and PairingOffer.secret is a plain String (by design, since it is the QR payload) that is Clone and never wiped. Also, sha256() and SecretKey::public() fall back to all-zero output if the resolver lacks the primitive. That cannot happen with use-sha2 and use-curve25519 enabled, but it would fail silently rather than loudly.

seal() does not enforce the 4 MiB cap itself. It is enforced before seal by wire::codec finish() (codec.rs:88, MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES), and encode_host is the only producer (conn.rs:108). open() checks the cap before decrypting or growing each chunk, with no overflow (out.len() <= max_plain and len - 16 <= 65519), and refuses a truncated length, a length below the tag size and trailing bytes. conn.rs:205-208 sets tungstenite's max_message_size to max_wire_bytes(4 MiB), so memory is capped before decryption.

The clients.json write is temp file + fsync + rename (atomic), but the parent directory is not fsynced after the rename, and the temp file gets the default mode. The contents are public keys, names and scopes only, so no secret is exposed. A corrupt file, a bad entry, a duplicate id or key, more than 32 clients, or an unknown schema all refuse to open and are never written, because a store is never built for them.

findings.issue: validate_binds checks a.ip().is_unspecified(), which is false for IPv4-mapped forms. Input binds=[[::ffff:0.0.0.0]:7000] (or [::ffff:0:0]) -> validate_binds returns Ok and start() calls TcpListener::bind. On Linux, Rust std leaves IPV6_V6ONLY at the kernel default (0) and __inet6_bind accepts a mapped INADDR_ANY, so the host listens on every IPv4 interface. G5 says unspecified addresses are refused before any socket call with no override; the review brief named mapped forms explicitly. Probe (scratch crate, Windows): is_unspecified=false, to_canonical()=0.0.0.0; on Windows the bind fails (os error 10049) only because V6ONLY defaults to 1 there, so desktop-on-Linux and orchestrad (H2) are the exposed hosts. Fix: a.ip().to_canonical().is_unspecified() (or refuse any v4-mapped bind), and add [::ffff:0.0.0.0]:0 to unspecified_addresses_are_refused_before_any_socket_call. The Linux bind result comes from reading the kernel source, not from a run (no Linux host here).

link-call workers are detached: stop() joins the accept and connection threads but not the up to 8 per-connection dispatch workers, so stop() can return while a remote land/answer/start_session is still running in wire::dispatch and changing Sessions. It was accepted before stop, so it is not a privilege bypass, but G5 says stop joins the threads. Before the P3b disable toggle, consider holding the JoinHandles in the connection and joining them on exit.

Revoke-during-connect window: handshake() checks client_by_key and then run() sends welcome and the full snapshot before the first per-pass revocation check. A revoke landing in those microseconds still sends one snapshot, then error revoked. Events can also go out up to one ~25 ms pass after a revoke or a read-scope removal, because current is read before poll(). Both are bounded and need no change now.

PendingPairing.client_name is the raw hello string, which can be up to MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES (4 MiB) and is passed to on_pairing_request unclipped; the store clips it on add. Only a psk holder can reach this. The P3b dialog should get the clipped name.

Pre-auth memory: tungstenite max_message_size is max_wire_bytes(4 MiB) from the upgrade on, so before Noise each socket can make the host buffer about 4 MiB for a version frame that is then refused for being over 1 KiB. That is bounded at about 16 x 4 MiB by the connection cap. A small cap until the handshake completes would tighten it. Also, upgrade and handshake each get their own handshake_timeout, so a pre-auth socket can hold a slot for about 2 x 10 s, and two IPs at 10 per minute can fill all 16 slots (an inherent DoS on an exposed bind).

RateLimiter refuses every new source once 1024 sources have hit within the window. That is fine on IPv4 LAN or loopback, but on an IPv6 bind (P3b) one attacker rotating /64 addresses locks out legitimate new sources for up to a minute. Consider keying IPv6 by /64.

confirm_pairing/await_confirmation race: if the confirm deadline fires and confirm_pairing removes the pending entry before the receiver is dropped, the sync_channel(1) send succeeds, so the client is stored but never gets a welcome. The host did confirm it, so this is benign, but it contradicts the comment at line 410. Also, a panic inside conn::serve would skip connection_closed and leak a connection slot; a drop guard would make that robust (no reachable panic found).
